about: IMAGE SETS for scripts/identify_web_images.py in benchmark mode.
A SET is one species and up to three photographs of it. The condition matrix runs the
same set at one, two and three photographs, and at two different slot-3 organ tags, so
everything that moves between conditions is the request rather than the pictures.
`expectedHerbId` is the card a CORRECT identification should reach, and null means the
correct answer is NO CARD — the Seed Shelf. Those entries are not filler: the share of
real scans that land on the shelf is a measurement nobody here has made, and a benchmark
built only from deck species would report a card-match rate of 100% by construction and
tell us nothing about the outcome a stranger is most likely to meet.
`sameIndividual` is the honesty field and every entry below says false. A Commons
category returns photographs of DIFFERENT PLANTS taken by different people, so a set
built from one is a fair test of 'does the deck find this species' and a WEAK test of
'do three views of one plant beat two' — the provider is being handed three specimens,
which is not what a player sends. Setting `files` to a hand-picked series by one
photographer of one plant, and `sameIndividual` to true, is what makes the photo-count
result mean what it says. Run with RESOLVE=1 to list a category's files and pick from
them; it spends nothing.
`organs` are the tags sent with photographs 1, 2 and 3. They describe what the
photographs ACTUALLY SHOW, so the p3tag condition is a true organ tag rather than a
guess — which is the only way the comparison against p3auto measures the tag.
`pilot: true` marks the six sets of the first run, selected with PILOT=1. They are two
easy deck species, two known-hard deck species, one easy off-deck species and one
off-deck species that is a lookalike of a deck card — a spread of difficulty rather than
a spread of coverage, because the first thing a six-set run can tell you is whether an
aggregate is being carried by one or two hard species. The genus-card and Field Card
paths are deliberately NOT in the pilot: they each exercise one eligibility branch and
neither is where the accuracy question lives.

sets.why: An easy, distinctive deck species. The control: if this moves between conditions, the harness is measuring noise.
Easy in flower, and the species whose SECTIONS the normaliser deliberately keeps apart. A provider answer of 'Taraxacum sect. Taraxacum' should open the card; 'sect. Erythrosperma' should not.
The species that produced 'it will not identify dock'. Five real photographs scored 0.616 to 0.303, which is why outcomeFor reads rank rather than an absolute score. Re-measure that spread.
The relatedOnly case. A field violet came back as five Viola species, none of them sororia. Measures how often the deck's violet is reachable at all.
The one pendingCuration card. Every match through it is tagged legacyGenus, so this set measures how much live coverage that temporary scope is actually carrying before it is curated away.
Oxalis dillenii is a separate species the deck must not rewrite to stricta. Measures how often the leading answer is the congener.
A real species inside a spp. card. A correct answer here is a genusCard match, which is confirmable — a different eligibility from every other deck set.

A Field Card species. The matcher indexes CATALOGUE rather than the printed deck, so this should be confirmable — and it was not before that change. A regression here is the scanner telling a player a card they can read is not a card.

The Seed Shelf case named in CLAUDE.md: the deck carries C. bursa-pastoris and rubella is a different species that belongs on the shelf. Also the hardest of them, because the two are genuinely difficult apart.
An extremely common lawn plant with no card and no deck congener. The plain Seed Shelf outcome, and the one a stranger scanning their own garden is most likely to hit.
Wild carrot: no card, and half of the lookalike pair below. Its own identification is the baseline the hemlock result is read against.

Poison hemlock, the classic dangerous lookalike for wild carrot. Neither is a card, so nothing here can reach a discovery — what is being measured is whether the identifier confuses the two, because the shelf entry prints the name the provider gave and a reader will act on it.
An off-deck Rumex. The deck holds TWO Rumex cards, so a correct outcome is relatedOnly naming both — never a confirmable obtusifolius. This is the set that would catch the matcher over-reaching.
